lead: A lamp turns electrical power into light, and its efficacy is the light out per watt in, in lumens per watt (lm/W). Filament, halogen, gas-discharge and LED sources differ in that number, in colour, in how fast they start and in how long they last. A headlamp also has to meet strict technical demands: light far down the road without dazzling anyone. This chapter covers the photometric units, how each source makes light, how lighting developed, and the lamp units built round the sources. Only a few universities teach this topic.

blocks.text: Light is measured in four linked units. Luminous flux Φ is the total light output, in lumens (lm). Luminous intensity I is flux per unit solid angle in one direction, in candela (cd = lm/sr). Illuminance E is the flux falling on a surface, in lux (lx = lm/m²). Luminance is intensity per unit projected area of a source or surface, in cd/m²; it is what the eye sees as brightness. Efficacy is η = Φ/P, with P the electrical power in W.
On the road, illuminance falls with the square of distance from the lamp:

blocks.where: E is the illuminance in lux on a surface facing the lamp, I the intensity of the beam in that direction in candela, and d the distance in metres.

blocks.text: Spreading the same flux over a wider beam lowers the intensity in each direction, so a lamp with more lumens does not always light the road better. Lamp makers quote a bulb's power and flux at its test voltage, 13.2 V for a 12 V lamp.

Incandescence: current heats a tungsten filament until it glows, about 2700 K in a vacuum bulb, giving 10–15 lm/W. Most of the power leaves as infrared heat. A halogen lamp adds iodine or bromine to the fill gas. Evaporated tungsten combines with the halogen near the hot quartz glass and is carried back to the filament, the halogen cycle, so the bulb stays clear and the filament can run hotter, about 3000–3200 K, at about 20–30 lm/W.

Gas discharge: a high-voltage pulse, about 20 kV from the ballast, strikes an arc through xenon gas between two electrodes; metal salts then vaporise and give most of the light. A 35 W HID (xenon) lamp gives about 3000 lm, 80–90 lm/W, bluish-white, but needs the ballast and a few seconds to reach full output. Electroluminescence: in an LED, electrons and holes recombine at a semiconductor junction and release photons; a blue chip with a phosphor coat gives white light. LEDs give about 90–110 lm/W at the lamp, start instantly, last the life of the car and need a constant-current driver and a heat sink. A laser headlamp aims blue laser diodes at a phosphor to make a very small, very bright spot, used to extend the high beam.

sections.h3: Development, technical demands and lamp units

blocks.text: Car lamps went from acetylene and oil lamps to vacuum filament bulbs, then to two-filament bulbs giving main and dipped beam from one lamp. Halogen bulbs arrived in the 1960s, xenon HID in the early 1990s, full-LED headlamps in the late 2000s, and laser high beams in the mid-2010s. Each step gave more light for less power.

The technical demands on a headlamp are: enough light far down the road; a dipped beam with a sharp cut-off so no light rises into oncoming eyes; fixed colours; resistance to vibration, heat and water; long life; and type approval of the lamp and bulb together. The dipped beam is asymmetric. In India, where traffic keeps left, the cut-off rises on the left to light the kerb and road signs, and stays low on the right, towards oncoming traffic; in right-hand-traffic countries it is mirrored.

A source is shaped into a beam by a lamp unit. A reflector lamp uses a shaped mirror, with a clear or fluted lens; a free-form reflector divides the mirror into facets that each place light in one part of the pattern. A projector lamp uses an ellipsoidal reflector, a shield and a lens: the shield cuts off the upper light at the focus, and the lens images its edge onto the road as the sharp cut-off line.

examples.question: A halogen headlamp uses a 55 W bulb giving 1500 lm. An LED headlamp gives 2000 lm for 20 W. Both are rated at the 13.2 V test voltage. Find the efficacy of each and the current each draws.
steps: The LED gives 2000 − 1500 = 500 lm (33%) more flux for 35 W and 2.65 A less.
examples.answer: Halogen 27.3 lm/W at 4.17 A; LED 100 lm/W at 1.52 A: 33% more light for 2.65 A less current.

examples.question: The brightest point of a dipped beam has an intensity of 20 000 cd. Find the illuminance on a sign facing the car at 25 m and at 50 m.
steps: Doubling the distance cuts the illuminance to a quarter: 32 ÷ 4 = 8 lx.
examples.answer: 32 lx at 25 m and 8 lx at 50 m.

traps: Lumen, candela and lux are not interchangeable: lumen is total output, candela is output in one direction, lux is light falling on a surface.
Forgetting the square in E = I ÷ d²: at twice the distance the illuminance is a quarter, not a half.
HID xenon is not an LED: it is an arc lamp that needs a high-voltage ballast and a warm-up.
Halogen efficacy is 20–30 lm/W, not 80; about 80–90 lm/W is HID.
Reversing the asymmetric dip for India: the cut-off rises on the left (kerb side) and stays low on the right.

quiz.q: Define luminous flux and give its unit.
quiz.a: Luminous flux is the total light output of a source, weighted for the eye's sensitivity; unit lumen (lm).

quiz.q: Why does a halogen lamp last longer and run brighter than a plain tungsten lamp?
quiz.a: The halogen cycle carries evaporated tungsten back to the filament instead of letting it blacken the glass, so the filament can run hotter, giving more light per watt, and lasts longer.

quiz.q: A 35 W HID lamp gives 2800 lm. Find its efficacy.
A 1000 lm LED and a 1500 lm halogen bulb are fitted in the same reflector. Which lights the road better, and why?
quiz.a: With the same reflector the beam shape is the same, so intensity and illuminance scale with the flux: the halogen gives about 1500/1000 = 1.5 times the light on the road. The LED's higher efficacy only means it draws less current.

quiz.q: Name the three principles by which car lamps make light.
quiz.a: Incandescence (filament and halogen), gas discharge (HID xenon) and electroluminescence (LED).

quiz.q: What does the shield do in a projector headlamp?
quiz.a: It blocks the upper part of the light at the reflector's second focus; the lens images the shield's edge onto the road as a sharp cut-off, so oncoming drivers are not dazzled.

quiz.q: A beam of 12 000 cd lights a pedestrian 40 m ahead. Find the illuminance.

beyond: Matrix LED and pixel headlamps switch many small sources one by one, and micro-LED arrays are in research. Lamp makers test every design on a goniophotometer that maps intensity in every direction. Search terms: matrix LED headlamp, laser headlamp, goniophotometer, headlamp type approval.
